sdoering · Nov 20, 2026

While this is a real operating constraint I am missing evidence of a major airline problem. The article turns normal flight planning into something much more dramatic.

Step climbing is routine on long-haul aircraft, including widebodies. A fuel-heavy aircraft initially cruises lower, then climbs as it gets lighter. It isn’t continuously struggling uphill for hours. Lower than the eventual cruise altitude does not necessarily mean below the optimum altitude as the optimum changes with weight if my understanding is correct. And yes, the article acknowledges this, but then (imho misleadingly) treats those initial lower levels as an automatic efficiency penalty.

Also, yes, the XLR’s extra weight does involve trade-offs. But airlines evaluate fuel consumption over the whole mission, not how quickly an aircraft reaches 37,000 feet.

The article does not establish that carriers are experiencing this systematically. Its “2.5% per hour” fuel penalty has no clear calculation or baseline, and the claim that climbing above 32,000 feet leaves only “a few knots” of safe margin is presented without supporting performance data.

The “coffin corner” framing is particularly sensational.

Step climbing is a normal procedure for any long haul flight. It's not unique to the A321XLR. It's just at the bad end of the spectrum because it's a smaller aircraft, with a higher, less efficient wing load, compared to the usual long haulers like the 777 and 787. ajross · Nov 20, 2026

No, the way the physics works is that the distance/energy efficiency varies (to first order anyway) with the air temperature. And it's colder the higher you get, up to this funny layer called the tropopause where the temperature (somewhat oddly) stops varying with altitude at all. And this altitude varies a little, but is always right around 36kft.

So as soon as jets were powerful enough to get there, they all wanted to fly at the tropopause, but no higher.

YJ57-P-3 · Nov 20, 2026

This is profoundly not a new thing. Aircraft with high ceilings and high gross weights normally have to do some form of step climb if they're taking off near max takeoff weight.

B-52Ds with the 'big belly' modification and external stores flying missions from Guam to Viet Nam in the 1960s/70s would struggle to 20,000 ft or so, then would slowly climb to more normal cruise altitudes as they burned fuel until they had lost enough weight that they could maintain best economy cruise (a variable, but usually something like .85 Mach above 30,000) ft.
